candidates.statement: 4.1 Purpose Chapter 4 provides guidance on the communication of important safety information relating to medicinal products. It applies to the Agency and to Marketing Authorization Holders (MAHs) and should be read as part of the broader GVP framework governing quality systems, signal management, risk management planning, product information changes, periodic safety reporting and additional risk minimization measures.
candidates.context: Where important new or evolving safety concerns are identified, the quality, timing and clarity of communication can directly influence clinical decisions, patient adherence, risk minimization behaviour, adverse event reporting and public confidence in medicines regulation. A poorly timed or poorly framed message may create avoidable panic, encourage inappropriate discontinuation of beneficial treatment, or fail to achieve the intended change in behaviour. This chapter defines the roles and responsibilities and procedural aspects of safety communication process in Nigeria. The guidance is consistent with internationally recognised standards for safety communication and aligns with established best practices as described in EMA GVP Module IX . It is adapted to support effective implementation within the Nigerian regulatory framework.

candidates.statement: 4.7 Target Audiences The primary target audiences for safety communication should be patients, caregivers and healthcare professionals who prescribe, dispense, administer, recommend, handle or use medicinal products.
candidates.context: i. Ensuring that relevant pharmacovigilance, medical, regulatory and quality personnel are trained on applicable communication procedures. Healthcare professionals and patients/caregivers constitute the primary target audiences for safety communication, given their direct role in the safe use of medicinal products, implementation of risk minimisation measures, monitoring, and reporting of safety-related concerns.

candidates.statement: 4.9.2.2 A DHPC is not a response to an individual enquiry and should not be used as routine promotional or educational material. It is a focused safety intervention intended to support patient protection and regulatory implementation.
candidates.context: 4.9.2.1 A Direct Healthcare Professional Communication (DHPC) is a targeted regulatory communication used to deliver important safety information directly to individual healthcare professionals where there is a need for immediate awareness, specific action, or a change in clinical or dispensing practice in relation to a medicinal product. 4.9.2.3 The preparation of a DHPC should involve cooperation between the MAH and the Agency.

candidates.statement: When using rapid or digital communication channels, special attention should be paid to governance, accuracy, version control, and consistency with official regulatory messages. Faster channels should not compromise scientific accuracy, regulatory oversight or clarity of recommended actions.
candidates.context: The Agency recognises the role of digital reporting and communication tools, including the Med Safety App, which supports the reporting of suspected adverse reactions and may contribute to improved accessibility of pharmacovigilance reporting by healthcare professionals, MAHs and consumers. 4.9.7 Bulletins, Newsletters and Circulars Bulletins, newsletters and circulars may be used to provide periodic updates on the safety and effectiveness of medicinal products, communicate lessons from pharmacovigilance data, reinforce reporting obligations, and highlight recent regulatory actions or product information changes.

candidates.statement: 4.10.2 Where safety communication forms part of an additional risk minimisation measure, it should be planned, documented and evaluated in a manner consistent with the overall risk management plan and relevant pharmacovigilance obligations.
candidates.context: 4.10.1 In addition to product information, safety communication tools may be used as part of broader risk minimisation activities. Depending on the nature of the risk, these may include educational materials, controlled access information, patient alert cards, checklists, prescribing guides, dispensing guides, monitoring tools or targeted training materials. 4.11 Evaluation of Effectiveness of Safety Communication Safety communication is considered effective when the intended message is received, understood and acted upon by the target audience in the way intended, and when the communication contributes to safer medicine use or improved risk control.

candidates.statement: A research-based or structured evaluation approach should be used where appropriate, especially for high-impact or recurring safety issues.

The Agency and MAHs should maintain written procedures that describe how safety communications are initiated, reviewed, approved, disseminated, updated, archived and evaluated.

Depending on the type of communication, review may involve pharmacovigilance, medical, regulatory, legal, quality and communications functions, provided that such review does not delay urgent patient safety action. 4.14 Conclusion This Chapter provides a strong and operationally useful framework for safety communication under the NAFDAC GVP system. It improves clarity of language, strengthens regulatory expectations, standardises roles, and embeds safety communication within the wider pharmacovigilance quality and risk management architecture. Most importantly, it recognises that medicine safety information only achieves public health value when it is communicated in a timely, coordinated, understandable and actionable manner.
